lesson.title: From Grams to Formula: Building an Empirical Formula from Real Data
lesson.summary: Determining an empirical formula from real data means converting measured element masses into moles, then finding the smallest whole number ratio between them.
lesson.body:
An empirical formula gives the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound, and finding one from real experimental data means starting with raw numbers from data collection, typically masses of each element in a sample, and working backward to that ratio. This connects percent composition and empirical formula in the direction you actually use in the lab: rather than being handed a formula and asked to calculate percent composition from it, you are handed masses, or percentages, from an experiment and asked to reconstruct the formula that produced them.

The procedure has a fixed shape. Convert the mass of each element to moles using its molar mass, since moles, not mass, are what reflect the actual ratio of atoms. Then divide every mole value by the smallest one in the set, which normalizes the smallest amount to exactly 1 and expresses the others relative to it. If those ratios come out close to whole numbers, round them, and if they come out close to a simple fraction like 0.5, multiply every ratio by the appropriate small whole number, 2 for halves, 3 for thirds, until all of them land on whole numbers.

Suppose a 100.0 g sample of a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen is analyzed and found to contain 40.00 g of carbon, 6.71 g of hydrogen, and 53.29 g of oxygen. Moles of each element: carbon, 40.00 g / 12.01 g/mol = 3.331 mol; hydrogen, 6.71 g / 1.008 g/mol = 6.657 mol; oxygen, 53.29 g / 16.00 g/mol = 3.331 mol.

Dividing every value by the smallest, 3.331 mol: carbon becomes 3.331 / 3.331 = 1.000, oxygen becomes 3.331 / 3.331 = 1.000, and hydrogen becomes 6.657 / 3.331 = 1.999, which rounds cleanly to 2. The mole ratio of carbon to hydrogen to oxygen is 1 to 2 to 1, giving the empirical formula CH2O. This is, in fact, the real empirical formula of glucose, C6H12O6, whose actual molecular formula is a whole number multiple, six times, of this simplest ratio.

Notice how much rides on the quality of the original data collection. A small error in one measured mass, a sample that had not been fully dried before weighing, or a reaction that had not gone to completion before the masses were recorded, would shift the mole ratios away from clean whole numbers and could easily lead to the wrong empirical formula entirely. This is exactly why the earlier chapters in this unit matter here: a molecular equation written correctly, a reaction predicted accurately, a precipitate identified with confidence, and a titration run with a properly standardized solution are all, in the end, ways of making sure the numbers that eventually go into a calculation like this one are numbers you can actually trust.
